newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh PM warns opposition of by-elections.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh PM warns opposition of by-elections.

text.p: Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina said on Friday she might call by-elections if boycotting opposition legislators did not return to parliament.
"If the opposition remains absent from parliament for 90 consecutive working days their seats will fall vacant and by-elections will be called to fill them out," Hasina said.
She was participating in a discussion on the "26th Homecoming Day" -- the anniversary of the day her father Sheikh Mujibur Rahman returned following the country's independence.
Bangladesh, formerly East Pakistan, emerged as an independent country on December 16, 1971, and Mujib, jailed in the former West Pakistan for over nine months, came back home on January 10, 1972.

Legislators of the main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), headed by former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia, walked out during parliament's last session in November, and there is no sign they will return when the next sitting begins on January 15.
"I will not run parliament like you did, and will follow the constitution to fill out vacant seats immediately," the prime minister said.
While in opposition, Hasina's Awami League boycotted parliament from February 1994 and the Awami legislators formally resigned in December that year.
But the BNP did not call by-elections and stayed in power until March 1996, when an Awami-led opposition uprising forced Khaleda to resign.
The Awami League won parliamentary elections in June, regaining power 21 years after Mujib was killed in a 1975 army coup.
"I will follow the constitution. I don't want to perpetuate my rule by taking advantage of the opposition not being in parliament," Hasina said.
"The BNP's walkout was like the act of a trade union," the prime minister was quoted by reporters as saying.
On Friday morning, Hasina laid wreaths at the portrait of Mujib at his Dhaka home, now a museum.
The BNP walked out on November 10, complaining of "repression and arrest of BNP leaders and workers in a motivated police crackdown".
"The allegations are not true," the prime minister said.
Referring to the BNP's threats to topple her government, Hasina said: "I have full confidence in the people. They are the best judge."
The animosity between the two women politicians seemed to intensify after former president Hossain Mohammad Ershad, a staunch foe of Khaleda, was released on Thursday after six years in jail.
Khaleda alleged Ershad's freedom was the "result of an unholy alliance between his Jatiya Party and the Awami League".
Ershad denied the charge, and said the BNP, which came to power after Ershad was toppled in an uprising in 1990, had forced him into jail "because it was afraid of my popularity".
